claim: Centrioles are cylindrical cell organelles with a ninefold symmetric peripheral microtubule array that is essential to template cilia and flagella.
source: Centrioles are cylindrical cell organelles with a ninefold symmetric peripheral microtubule array that is essential to template cilia and flagella.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about centriole structure and function.

claim: Centrioles are built around a central cartwheel assembly that is organized through homo-oligomerization of the centriolar protein SAS-6.
source: They are built around a central cartwheel assembly that is organized through homo-oligomerization of the centriolar protein SAS-6, but whether SAS-6 self-assembly can dictate cartwheel and thereby centriole symmetry is unclear.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about centriole structure and SAS-6's role, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Leishmania major SAS-6 crystallizes as a 9-fold symmetric cartwheel.
source: Here we show that Leishmania major SAS-6 crystallizes as a 9-fold symmetric cartwheel and provide the X-ray structure of this assembly at a resolution of 3.5 Å.
evidence: This is supported by experimental crystallography data presented in the manuscript, including Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The X-ray structure of the Leishmania major SAS-6 cartwheel assembly was determined at a resolution of 3.5 Å.
source: Here we show that Leishmania major SAS-6 crystallizes as a 9-fold symmetric cartwheel and provide the X-ray structure of this assembly at a resolution of 3.5 Å.
evidence: This is directly supported by crystallographic data in Table 1 showing resolution of 66.9–3.5/4.2 Å.

claim: Oligomerization of Leishmania SAS-6 can be inhibited by a small molecule in vitro.
source: We furthermore demonstrate that oligomerization of Leishmania SAS-6 can be inhibited by a small molecule in vitro and provide indications for its binding site.
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS and NMR data showing PK9119 inhibits SAS-6 oligomerization (Figure 3).

claim: SAS-6 can impose cartwheel symmetry on its own.
source: Our results firmly establish that SAS-6 can impose cartwheel symmetry on its own and indicate how this process might occur mechanistically in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure showing ninefold symmetric rings formed by SAS-6 alone.

claim: Inhibition of SAS-6 oligomerization by small molecules is feasible.
source: Importantly, our data also provide a proof-of-principle that inhibition of SAS-6 oligomerization by small molecules is feasible.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PK9119 inhibition experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Eukaryotic flagella and cilia have essential roles in cell locomotion, fluid movement, and sensing.
source: Eukaryotic flagella and cilia have essential roles in cell locomotion, fluid movement, and sensing.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about flagella and cilia function.

claim: Formation of flagella and cilia strictly requires the presence of centrioles.
source: Their formation strictly requires the presence of centrioles, cylindrical organelles with a radially ninefold symmetric, peripheral microtubule array (Bettencourt-Dias and Glover, 2007; Azimzadeh and Marshall, 2010; Gonczy, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: During ciliogenesis/flagellogenesis, centrioles dock to the cell membrane via their distal ends and nucleate the flagellar/ciliar axoneme from their microtubule array.
source: During ciliogenesis/flagellogenesis, centrioles (then referred to as basal bodies) dock to the cell membrane via their distal ends and nucleate the flagellar/ciliar axoneme from their microtubule array (Sherwin and Gull, 1989; Dawe et al., 2007; Ishikawa and Marshall, 2011; Avasthi and Marshall, 2012; Chemes, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The symmetry and diameter of centrioles is, to a large extent, established through scaffolding by the centriolar cartwheel.
source: The symmetry and diameter of centrioles (and thereby of flagella/cilia) is, to a large extent, established through scaffolding by the centriolar cartwheel, a structure with a central ring-like hub and nine radially projecting spokes that contact the peripheral centriolar microtubules (Azimzadeh and Marshall, 2010; Brito et al., 2012; Gonczy, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The cartwheel is a structure with a central ring-like hub and nine radially projecting spokes that contact the peripheral centriolar microtubules.
source: The symmetry and diameter of centrioles (and thereby of flagella/cilia) is, to a large extent, established through scaffolding by the centriolar cartwheel, a structure with a central ring-like hub and nine radially projecting spokes that contact the peripheral centriolar microtubules (Azimzadeh and Marshall, 2010; Brito et al., 2012; Gonczy, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing cartwheel structure.

claim: The cartwheel is organized through the homo-oligomerization of the highly conserved centriolar protein SAS-6.
source: The cartwheel is organized through the homo-oligomerization of the highly conserved centriolar protein SAS-6 (Nakazawa et al., 2007; Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SAS-6 has a coiled-coil domain that forms a rod-like parallel dimer.
source: High-resolution crystal structures of zebrafish and C. reinhardtii SAS-6 fragments together with biochemical and biophysical characterizations (Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011) demonstrated that two dimerization interfaces in SAS-6 mediate this oligomerization: a coiled-coil domain that forms a rod-like parallel dimer; and a globular N-terminal domain that forms a curved head-to-head dimer.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: SAS-6 has a globular N-terminal domain that forms a curved head-to-head dimer.
source: High-resolution crystal structures of zebrafish and C. reinhardtii SAS-6 fragments together with biochemical and biophysical characterizations (Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011) demonstrated that two dimerization interfaces in SAS-6 mediate this oligomerization: a coiled-coil domain that forms a rod-like parallel dimer; and a globular N-terminal domain that forms a curved head-to-head dimer.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: In SAS-6 models, the N-terminal head domains constitute the cartwheel hubs from which the coiled-coil rods project to form the cartwheel spokes.
source: In these models, the N-terminal head domains constitute the cartwheel hubs from which the coiled-coil rods project to form the cartwheel spokes (Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on modeling studies cited in previous literature.

claim: No high-resolution structure of the SAS-6 cartwheel was available prior to this study.
source: However, so far, no high-resolution structure of the SAS-6 cartwheel is available.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: A previous EM study with recombinant SAS-6 revealed cartwheel-like assemblies with an eightfold, not a ninefold symmetry.
source: Another, higher resolution, EM study with recombinant SAS-6 revealed cartwheel-like assemblies with an eightfold, not a ninefold symmetry (van Breugel et al., 2011), while a third EM study showed the presence of SAS-6 tetramers (Gopalakrishnan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous EM study.

claim: A previous EM study showed the presence of SAS-6 tetramers.
source: Another, higher resolution, EM study with recombinant SAS-6 revealed cartwheel-like assemblies with an eightfold, not a ninefold symmetry (van Breugel et al., 2011), while a third EM study showed the presence of SAS-6 tetramers (Gopalakrishnan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous EM study.

claim: Available biochemical and biophysical data do not provide evidence for efficient cartwheel formation by SAS-6 in solution.
source: Furthermore, the available biochemical and biophysical data do not provide evidence for efficient cartwheel formation by SAS-6 in solution (Gopalakrishnan et al., 2010; Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011), raising the question of whether SAS-6 alone is sufficient to organize ninefold symmetric cartwheels and, if so, under what conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous biochemical and biophysical studies.

claim: SAS-6 is a highly conserved protein that is found in all eukaryotes that have cilia/flagella during some of their life-cycle stages.
source: SAS-6 is a highly conserved protein that is found in all eukaryotes that have cilia/flagella during some of their life-cycle stages (Carvalho-Santos et al., 2010; Hodges et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on SAS-6 conservation.

claim: Inhibiting SAS-6 self-assembly by point mutations in vivo abolishes the formation of centrioles.
source: Inhibiting SAS-6 self-assembly by point mutations in vivo abolishes the formation of centrioles (Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011; Lettman et al., 2013) and thereby flagella (van Breugel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vivo studies.

claim: Inhibiting SAS-6 self-assembly by point mutations in vivo abolishes the formation of flagella.
source: Inhibiting SAS-6 self-assembly by point mutations in vivo abolishes the formation of centrioles (Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011; Lettman et al., 2013) and thereby flagella (van Breugel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous in vivo study.

claim: Targeting SAS-6 oligomerization by inhibitors could be a strategy to disable flagellogenesis in organisms that cause human disease and rely on flagella for their pathogenicity.
source: Thus, targeting SAS-6 oligomerization by inhibitors could be a strategy to disable flagellogenesis in organisms that cause human disease and rely on flagella for their pathogenicity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the known role of SAS-6 in flagellogenesis.

claim: Trypanosomatids consist of parasitic, eukaryotic protozoa with a single flagellum.
source: They consist of parasitic, eukaryotic protozoa with a single flagellum and comprise members that cause major human diseases, such as sleeping sickness (Trypanosoma brucei), Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi), and Leishmaniasis (Leishmania spec.) (Simpson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Trypanosomatids, supported by citation.

claim: Trypanosomatids comprise members that cause major human diseases, such as sleeping sickness, Chagas disease, and Leishmaniasis.
source: They consist of parasitic, eukaryotic protozoa with a single flagellum and comprise members that cause major human diseases, such as sleeping sickness (Trypanosoma brucei), Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi), and Leishmaniasis (Leishmania spec.) (Simpson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Trypanosomatid diseases, supported by citation.

claim: The flagellum of Trypanosomatids provides key roles in their life cycle through its multiple functions in essential cellular processes such as motility, signalling, sensing, and attachment.
source: Their flagellum provides key roles in this life cycle through its multiple functions in essential cellular processes such as motility, signalling, sensing, and attachment (Vaughan and Gull, 2003; Ralston et al., 2009; Gluenz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Trypanosomatid flagella.

claim: The flagellar pocket is the exclusive site of vesicular membrane traffic in Trypanosomatids.
source: Furthermore, the flagellar pocket, a membrane invagination from which the flagellum emerges, is the exclusive site of vesicular membrane traffic in these organisms (Overath et al., 1997; Landfear and Ignatushchenko, 2001; Field and Carrington, 2004, 2009; Overath and Engstler, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Trypanosomatid cell biology.

claim: Flagella have been demonstrated or are proposed to be key factors in the pathogenicity of Trypanosomatids.
source: It is therefore not surprising that flagella have been demonstrated or are proposed to be key factors in the pathogenicity of these organisms (Vaughan and Gull, 2003; Ralston et al., 2009; Gluenz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Trypanosomatid pathogenicity.

claim: The flagellum of Trypanosomatids is templated from centrioles (basal bodies).
source: As in other eukaryotes, the flagellum of the Trypanosomatids is templated from centrioles (basal bodies).
evidence: This is established knowledge about flagellum formation in Trypanosomatids.

claim: Tomographic EM studies demonstrated the presence of canonical, ninefold symmetric cartwheel structures in the centre of Trypanosomatid centrioles.
source: Tomographic EM studies demonstrated the presence of canonical, ninefold symmetric cartwheel structures in the centre of their centrioles (Lacomble et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous EM study.

claim: No high-resolution structures of SAS-6 homologues from Trypanosomatids were available prior to this study.
source: Currently, no high-resolution structures of SAS-6 homologues from Trypanosomatids are available, and it is unclear whether oligomerization of their SAS-6 homologues could be inhibited.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: The genomes of Trypanosoma brucei, Trypanosoma cruzi, and Leishmania major have been sequenced.
source: The genomes of Trypanosoma brucei, Trypanosoma cruzi, and Leishmania major have recently been sequenced (Berriman et al., 2005; El-Sayed et al., 2005; Ivens et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genome sequencing papers.

claim: BLAST searches identified the likely SAS-6 homologues in Trypanosoma brucei, Trypanosoma cruzi, and Leishmania major with similar domain architectures.
source: BLAST searches identified the likely SAS-6 homologues in these organisms with similar domain architectures (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and sequence identities to human SAS-6 of 21.0 ± 1.4% in 459 ± 21 aligned residues.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis and figures showing domain architecture.

claim: Trypanosomatid SAS-6 homologues have sequence identities to human SAS-6 of 21.0 ± 1.4% in 459 ± 21 aligned residues.
source: BLAST searches identified the likely SAS-6 homologues in these organisms with similar domain architectures (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and sequence identities to human SAS-6 of 21.0 ± 1.4% in 459 ± 21 aligned residues.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: Key residues in the N-terminal domains of Trypanosomatid SAS-6 homologues are well conserved compared to zebrafish SAS-6.
source: Multiple sequence alignment of their N-terminal domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) shows that key residues are well conserved compared to zebrafish SAS-6, the closest homologue of human SAS-6 for which high-resolution structures are available (van Breugel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Trypanosomatid SAS-6 homologues have long N-terminal extensions that vary in length and are poorly conserved.
source: Different from zebrafish SAS-6, they have long N-terminal extensions (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B) that vary in length and are poorly conserved.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment and domain architecture data shown in figures.

claim: The N-terminal extensions of Trypanosomatid SAS-6 hindered crystallization attempts.
source: Since these extensions hindered our crystallization attempts, we largely removed them in the constructs used in this manuscript.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental observations during crystallization.

claim: The part of the N-terminal extensions still present in crystallized constructs did not show electron density in crystal structures.
source: The part of the extensions still present did not show electron density in our crystal structures.
evidence: This is an observation from crystallographic data.

claim: The structure of L. major SAS-6 N-terminal domain (Lm SAS-697–274) was solved by X-ray crystallography to a resolution of 2.2 Å.
source: To elucidate the structural organization of L. major SAS-6, we solved the structure of its N-terminal domain (Lm SAS-697–274) by X-ray crystallography to a resolution of 2.2 Å (Table 1, Table 2; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data in Table 1 and structural figures.

claim: The asymmetric unit of the Lm SAS-697–274 crystal contained three molecules that were virtually identical to each other.
source: The asymmetric unit (ASU) of the crystal contained three molecules that were virtually identical to each other (139 ± 2 selected pairs superpose with an rmsd of 0.70 ± 0.13 Å in secondary structure matching).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic analysis data.

claim: L. major SAS-6 demonstrates a high similarity to previously solved SAS-6 structures.
source: Our structure demonstrates a high similarity of L. major SAS-6 to previously solved SAS-6 structures (Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011) (secondary structure matching to the D. rerio SAS-6 head domain results in an rmsd of 1.59 ± 0.09 Å with 133 ± 2 selected pairs).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data and citations to previous structures.

claim: The N-terminal domain of L. major SAS-6 consists of a 7-stranded β-barrel, capped by a helix-turn-helix motif.
source: Like these, the N-terminal domain of L. major SAS-6 consists of a 7-stranded β-barrel, capped by a helix-turn-helix motif, that forms a curved cross-handshake homo-dimer within the crystal through a highly conserved interaction interface (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The N-terminal domain of L. major SAS-6 forms a curved cross-handshake homo-dimer within the crystal through a highly conserved interaction interface.
source: Like these, the N-terminal domain of L. major SAS-6 consists of a 7-stranded β-barrel, capped by a helix-turn-helix motif, that forms a curved cross-handshake homo-dimer within the crystal through a highly conserved interaction interface (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and sequence conservation data shown in figures.

claim: In the L. major SAS-6 head-to-head dimer, phenylalanine 257 at the tip of the β-hairpin is inserted into a conserved hydrophobic pocket.
source: In this dimer, the β-hairpins formed by β-strands β6 and β7 pack antiparallelly against each other. Phenylalanine 257 at the tip of this hairpin is inserted into a conserved hydrophobic pocket that is constituted by the helix-turn-helix motif and the base of this hairpin in the B-C homo-dimer (formed by chain B and chain C in the crystal, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Dimerization of L. major SAS-6 N-terminal domain is observed in solution.
source: Dimerization is also observed in solution, as judged by equilibrium ultracentrifugation, and then depends on the presence of F257 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Dimerization of L. major SAS-6 N-terminal domain depends on the presence of F257.
source: Dimerization is also observed in solution, as judged by equilibrium ultracentrifugation, and then depends on the presence of F257 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data comparing wild-type and F257E mutant shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The measured KD of L. major SAS-6 head-to-head dimerization is approximately 600 μM.
source: The measured KD of this dimerization is ∼600 μM and therefore approximately 5- to 10-fold weaker than seen for other SAS-6 homologues (Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The KD of L. major SAS-6 head-to-head dimerization is approximately 5- to 10-fold weaker than seen for other SAS-6 homologues.
source: The measured KD of this dimerization is ∼600 μM and therefore approximately 5- to 10-fold weaker than seen for other SAS-6 homologues (Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of analytical ultracentrifugation data with cited previous studies.

claim: The structure of Lm SAS-697–320 F257E was solved by X-ray crystallography to a resolution of 2.9 Å.
source: However, by introducing the F257E mutation to strongly weaken head-to-head dimerization we managed to crystallize construct Lm SAS-697–320 F257E that contained the N-terminal head domain and the first seven heptad-repeats of the coiled-coil domain. We subsequently solved its X-ray structure to a resolution of 2.9 Å (Table 1; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: The asymmetric unit of the Lm SAS-697–320 F257E crystal contained four molecules that were highly similar to each other.
source: The asymmetric unit of the crystal contained four molecules that were highly similar to each other and superposed with an rmsd of 1.17 ± 0.50 Å in secondary structure matching with 165 ± 16 selected pairs.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic analysis data.

claim: The L. major SAS-6 coiled-coil domain is a parallel dimer.
source: The crystal structure revealed that the L. major SAS-6 coiled-coil domain is a parallel dimer and packs via conserved interactions against the N-terminal head-domains as seen in other SAS-6 homologues (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The L. major SAS-6 coiled-coil domain packs via conserved interactions against the N-terminal head-domains as seen in other SAS-6 homologues.
source: The crystal structure revealed that the L. major SAS-6 coiled-coil domain is a parallel dimer and packs via conserved interactions against the N-terminal head-domains as seen in other SAS-6 homologues (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and comparison with other SAS-6 structures shown in figures.

claim: L. major SAS-6 is highly similar to other SAS-6 homologues.
source: Thus, our structural analyses demonstrate that L. major SAS-6 is highly similar to other SAS-6 homologues.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural comparison data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the Lm SAS-697–274 crystal A–A homo-dimer, the Y215 sidechain is flipped into its own hydrophobic pocket resulting in the displacement of residue F257 of its homo-dimer partner.
source: However, in the A–A homo-dimer, the Y215 sidechain is flipped into its own hydrophobic pocket resulting in the displacement from this pocket of residue F257 of its homo-dimer partner (Figure 1C) probably weakening the interaction.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The closed Y215 conformation probably weakens the head-to-head dimerization interaction.
source: However, in the A–A homo-dimer, the Y215 sidechain is flipped into its own hydrophobic pocket resulting in the displacement from this pocket of residue F257 of its homo-dimer partner (Figure 1C) probably weakening the interaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: In the Lm SAS-697–320 F257E crystal octamer, residues Y215 are swung into their own hydrophobic pockets, while E257 point away from them.
source: Intriguingly, we found a similar arrangement in the Lm SAS-697–320 F257E crystal. The F257E mutation abolishes head-to-head dimerization in solution (Figure 1D), yet, in the crystal, due to the high protein and precipitant concentrations, some of the SAS-6 molecules present are found nevertheless in head-to-head dimers and form a curved octamer. In this octamer residues Y215 are also swung into their own hydrophobic pockets, while E257 point away from them (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The F257E mutation abolishes head-to-head dimerization of L. major SAS-6 in solution.
source: The F257E mutation abolishes head-to-head dimerization in solution (Figure 1D), yet, in the crystal, due to the high protein and precipitant concentrations, some of the SAS-6 molecules present are found nevertheless in head-to-head dimers and form a curved octamer.
evidence: This is supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The closed Y215 conformation corresponds to a low-affinity dimerization state of the head domains.
source: These data suggest that the closed Y215 conformation corresponds to a low-affinity dimerization state of the head domains and might therefore constitute a potential regulatory mechanism of SAS-6 oligomerization.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and biochemical data.

claim: The closed Y215 conformation might constitute a potential regulatory mechanism of SAS-6 oligomerization.
source: These data suggest that the closed Y215 conformation corresponds to a low-affinity dimerization state of the head domains and might therefore constitute a potential regulatory mechanism of SAS-6 oligomerization.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on structural observations.

claim: The presence of a dimerization-impaired state could explain the relatively low affinity of head-to-head dimerization of wild-type L. major SAS-6 in solution.
source: In solution, the presence of a dimerization-impaired state could also explain the relatively low affinity of head-to-head dimerization of wild-type L. major SAS-6 apparent in analytical ultracentrifugation (∼600 μM compared to 50–100 μM observed for other species) since other SAS-6 homologues do not have aromatic residues at the equivalent position of Y215 that could play such a role.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and biochemical data.

claim: Other SAS-6 homologues do not have aromatic residues at the equivalent position of Y215.
source: In solution, the presence of a dimerization-impaired state could also explain the relatively low affinity of head-to-head dimerization of wild-type L. major SAS-6 apparent in analytical ultracentrifugation (∼600 μM compared to 50–100 μM observed for other species) since other SAS-6 homologues do not have aromatic residues at the equivalent position of Y215 that could play such a role.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The measured KD of head-to-head dimerization of the Y215K mutant was approximately 200 μM.
source: The measured KD of head-to-head dimerization of the Y215K mutant was ∼200 μM and therefore approximately threefold lower than for the corresponding wild-type protein.
evidence: This is supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The KD of head-to-head dimerization of the Y215K mutant is approximately threefold lower than for the corresponding wild-type protein.
source: The measured KD of head-to-head dimerization of the Y215K mutant was ∼200 μM and therefore approximately threefold lower than for the corresponding wild-type protein.
evidence: This is supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Y215 acts to partially inhibit head-to-head dimerization of L. major SAS-6.
source: We conclude that Y215 acts to partially inhibit head-to-head dimerization of L. major SAS-6.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Y215K mutant data showing increased dimerization affinity.

claim: The presence of curved SAS-6 octamers in the crystal of the Lm SAS-697–320 F257E mutant suggests that wild-type versions of SAS-6 would adopt even larger assemblies.
source: The presence of curved SAS-6 octamers in the crystal of the Lm SAS-697–320 F257E mutant that is strongly impaired in its ability to form head-to-head dimers suggests that wild-type versions of SAS-6 would adopt even larger assemblies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of octamers in the F257E mutant crystal.

claim: The unit cell of the Lm SAS-697–320 crystal form contained three 9-fold symmetric SAS-6 rings with three SAS-6 dimers constituting the ASU.
source: Using the structure of the Lm SAS-697–274 B–C homo-dimer as a search model, a molecular replacement solution could be found that allowed the subsequent placement of the coiled-coil part present in the construct (Figure 2). The unit cell of the Lm SAS-697–320 crystal form contained three 9-fold symmetric SAS-6 rings with three SAS-6 dimers constituting the ASU.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and Figure 2.

claim: The three dimers in the ASU of the Lm SAS-697–320 crystal were highly similar to each other.
source: These three dimers were highly similar to each other and overlayed with an rmsd of 0.88 ± 0.29 Å in secondary structure matching with 357 ± 14 selected pairs.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic analysis data.

claim: No electron density was seen inside the SAS-6 rings in the Lm SAS-697–320 crystal.
source: No electron density was seen inside the SAS-6 rings.
evidence: This is an observation from crystallographic data.

claim: The inner diameters of the SAS-6 rings are approximately 19 nm.
source: The inner diameters of the SAS-6 rings are ∼19 nm and correspond well to the diameters of cartwheel hubs observed in vivo (Lacomble et al., 2009; Guichard et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by measurements from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: The inner diameters of the SAS-6 rings correspond well to the diameters of cartwheel hubs observed in vivo.
source: The inner diameters of the SAS-6 rings are ∼19 nm and correspond well to the diameters of cartwheel hubs observed in vivo (Lacomble et al., 2009; Guichard et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited EM studies of cartwheels in vivo.

claim: In the Lm SAS-697–320 crystal, SAS-6 rings are stacked onto each other.
source: In the crystal, SAS-6 rings are stacked onto each other. Neighbouring rings interact through inter-digitation of their coiled-coil domains in an antiparallel way (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neighbouring SAS-6 rings in the crystal interact through inter-digitation of their coiled-coil domains in an antiparallel way.
source: In the crystal, SAS-6 rings are stacked onto each other. Neighbouring rings interact through inter-digitation of their coiled-coil domains in an antiparallel way (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The structural model of Lm SAS-697–320 was confirmed by calculating a phased anomalous map using refined phases and amplitudes from a selenomethionine derivative dataset.
source: We confirmed our structural model by calculating a phased anomalous map using the refined phases based on our model and the amplitudes of an isomorphic dataset collected from crystals of the selenomethionine derivative (Figure 2B; Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by the phased anomalous map shown in Figure 2B and data in Table 3.

claim: Peaks in the phased anomalous map correlated with the positions of methionines in the structural model.
source: Peaks in this map correlated with the positions of methionines in our model.
evidence: This is supported by the phased anomalous map shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Under appropriate conditions, L. major SAS-6 can adopt ninefold symmetric rings that are highly similar to cartwheels observed in vivo.
source: Thus, under appropriate conditions, L. major SAS-6 can adopt ninefold symmetric rings that are highly similar to cartwheels observed in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the crystal structure data.

claim: Strong perturbations in chemical shifts are most consistent with compound PK9119 binding adjacent to the head-to-head dimerization interface of Lm SAS-697–274.
source: Strong perturbations in chemical shifts are most consistent with compound PK9119 ((5-bromo-7-ethyl-1H-indol-3-ylmethyl)-dimethyl-amine, Figure 3A) binding adjacent to the head-to-head dimerization interface of Lm SAS-697–274 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by NMR chemical shift perturbation data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Binding of PK9119 may alter the head-to-head dimerization interface by affecting the conformation of the helix-turn-helix motif.
source: Smaller, but significant shift changes indicate that binding may alter this interface by affecting the conformation of the helix-turn-helix motif that constitutes a part of it.
evidence: This is an inference based on NMR chemical shift perturbation data.

claim: Two aromatic side chains (F199, F212) are perturbed on binding of PK9119.
source: We also examined aromatic side chain 1H resonances of the Phe and Tyr residues using Cβ–Hδ correlation maps, which enabled us to identify two side-chains (F199, F212) that are perturbed on binding of PK9119 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: F199 and F212 cluster together around the helix-turn-helix motif.
source: These two side-chains cluster together around the helix-turn-helix motif.
evidence: This is based on mapping NMR perturbations onto the crystal structure shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HSQC chemical shift titration experiments with PK9119 and L. major SAS-697–274 F257E suggest a millimolar binding affinity.
source: HSQC chemical shift titration experiments with PK9119 and L. major SAS-697–274 F257E suggest a millimolar binding affinity; the low solubility of PK9119 in aqueous solutions and lack of a reference compound for competition binding assays makes more accurate KD determinations technically challenging.
evidence: This is based on NMR titration data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: L. major SAS-697–424 displayed a distribution of masses from that of the dimer up to >200 kDa consistent with a concentration driven self-association equilibrium.
source: L. major SAS-697–424 displayed a distribution of masses from that of the dimer up to >200 kDa consistent with a concentration driven self-association equilibrium.
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the presence of 1 mM PK9119, the maximal mass of L. major SAS-697–424 oligomers was almost halved.
source: In the presence of 1 mM PK9119 the maximal mass was almost halved.
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The F257E mutant of L. major SAS-697–424 displayed a constant mass of 71 kDa in the absence and presence of PK9119 consistent with the mass of a dimer.
source: The F257E mutant displayed a constant mass of 71 kDa in the absence and presence of PK9119 consistent with the mass of a dimer of L. major SAS-697–424.
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PK9119 partially affects head-to-head dimerization of L. major SAS-6.
source: When the runs were repeated in the presence of PK9119, we saw a clear shift in the elution volume for the wild-type but not the F257E SAS-6 construct towards smaller molecular weights and a decrease in the analysed mass from MALS, demonstrating that PK9119 partially affects head-to-head dimerization.
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Zebrafish SAS-6 oligomerization was affected by the presence of PK9119, although to a lesser extent than L. major SAS-6 oligomerization.
source: The results showed that zebrafish SAS-6 oligomerization was also affected by the presence of PK9119, although to a lesser extent than L. major SAS-6 oligomerization (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: PK9119 appears to be a general inhibitor of SAS-6 oligomerization in vitro with some preference for the L. major variant.
source: Thus, PK9119 appears to be a general inhibitor of SAS-6 oligomerization in vitro with some preference for the L. major variant, and represents a starting point for further screening of chemical analogs or fragment evolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on SEC-MALS data for both L. major and zebrafish SAS-6.

claim: PK9119 represents a starting point for further screening of chemical analogs or fragment evolution.
source: Thus, PK9119 appears to be a general inhibitor of SAS-6 oligomerization in vitro with some preference for the L. major variant, and represents a starting point for further screening of chemical analogs or fragment evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: The cartwheel is an early assembly intermediate of centrioles that participates in establishing their symmetry and diameter.
source: SAS-6 organizes the rotationally ninefold symmetric cartwheel (Nakazawa et al., 2007; Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011), an early assembly intermediate of centrioles that participates in establishing their symmetry and diameter (Nakazawa et al., 2007; Brito et al., 2012; Gonczy, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The current study provides the first unambiguous experimental evidence that SAS-6 is able to form ninefold symmetric cartwheels on its own.
source: However, we demonstrate that under high protein and precipitant concentrations, a L. major SAS-6 construct crystallized as ninefold symmetric rings with a diameter very similar to cartwheel hubs in vivo; this provides the first unambiguous experimental evidence that SAS-6 is able to form ninefold symmetric cartwheels on its own.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the crystal structure data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SAS-6 needs to be highly concentrated locally in order to be able to form cartwheels.
source: Our results suggest that SAS-6 needs to be highly concentrated locally in order to be able to form cartwheels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cartwheels only formed under high protein and precipitant concentrations in crystals.

claim: In vivo, SAS-6 is highly enriched at the site of centriole formation.
source: Intriguingly, in vivo, SAS-6 is indeed highly enriched at the site of centriole formation (Kleylein-Sohn et al., 2007; Strnad et al., 2007; Dammermann et al., 2008; Blachon et al., 2009; Sonnen et al., 2012; Lettman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vivo studies.

claim: In vivo, SAS-6 assembly occurs in the context of other essential centriole duplication factors, some of which can be found in a complex with SAS-6.
source: However, in vivo, SAS-6 assembly occurs in the context of other essential centriole duplication factors, some of which can be found in a complex with SAS-6 (Stevens et al., 2010; Tang et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on centriole duplication factors.

claim: It is likely that additional centriole proteins assist SAS-6 assembly in vivo.
source: It is therefore likely that additional centriole proteins assist SAS-6 assembly, especially in light of the fact that several studies (Gopalakrishnan et al., 2010; Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011), and our study presented here, have been unable to demonstrate efficient cartwheel assembly by SAS-6 in solution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of efficient cartwheel assembly in solution and the presence of SAS-6-interacting proteins in vivo.

claim: The interaction interfaces critical for ring formation (the head-to-head dimer interface and the head-domain–coiled-coil interface) are both relatively small.
source: The interaction interfaces that are critical for ring formation (i.e., the head-to-head dimer interface and the head-domain–coiled-coil interface) are both relatively small (Figures 1, 2; Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in Figures 1 and 2 and cited previous structures.

claim: In solution, SAS-6 oligomers are likely to show some 'wobble' that would make ring closure inefficient and assembled rings unstable.
source: In solution, SAS-6 oligomers are therefore likely to show some 'wobble' that would make ring closure inefficient and assembled rings unstable.
evidence: This is an inference based on the small size of the interaction interfaces.

claim: In the ring structure, both critical interfaces are similar in their orientations to those observed in crystals that did not crystallize as rings.
source: However, in our ring structure, both of these critical interfaces are similar in their orientations to those observed in the crystals of the Lm SAS-697–320 F257E and the Lm SAS-697–274 constructs that did not crystallize as rings (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ninefold symmetric ring formation might correspond to a weakly favored SAS-6 conformation that needs to be stabilized.
source: Thus, although clearly not occurring efficiently in solution, our data suggest that ninefold symmetric ring formation might correspond to a weakly favored SAS-6 conformation that needs to be stabilized.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that rings form in crystals but not efficiently in solution.

claim: In the crystal structure, rings are stabilized by crystal packing interactions.
source: In our crystal structure, rings are stabilized by crystal packing interactions and, in vivo, probably by SAS-6 interacting proteins.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure showing packing interactions.

claim: In vivo, SAS-6 rings are probably stabilized by SAS-6 interacting proteins.
source: In our crystal structure, rings are stabilized by crystal packing interactions and, in vivo, probably by SAS-6 interacting proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the crystal structure and knowledge of SAS-6-interacting proteins.

claim: SAS-6 is required for the faithful establishment of centriole symmetry, while not being the sole determinant of their ninefold symmetry in vivo.
source: This model could explain why SAS-6 is required for the faithful establishment of centriole symmetry, while not being the sole determinant of their ninefold symmetry in vivo (Nakazawa et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and cited previous studies.

claim: In basal bodies, cartwheels are stacked onto each other with a vertical distance between cartwheel hubs of approximately 8 nm.
source: In basal bodies, cartwheels are stacked onto each other with a vertical distance between cartwheel hubs of ∼8 nm (Guichard et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous EM study.

claim: In the crystal structure, the vertical distance between stacked cartwheel hubs was only approximately 4 nm.
source: Although we observed a similar stacking in our cartwheel hub structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), the corresponding distance was only ∼4 nm.
evidence: This is supported by measurements from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The packing interactions observed in the crystal are based on a non-conserved interface and are therefore unlikely to be of relevance in vivo.
source: Furthermore, although a comparable packing was previously observed in a crystal of the N-terminal head domain of zebrafish SAS-6 (van Breugel et al., 2011), the underlying packing interactions are based on a non-conserved interface and are therefore unlikely to be of relevance in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation analysis and comparison with previous structures.

claim: Recent EM tomograms suggest that ring stacking in vivo is based on parallel interactions between the SAS-6 coiled-coil stalks and vertical interactions of SAS-6 associated components at the periphery of centriolar cartwheels.
source: Recent EM tomograms of basal bodies from Trichonympha (Guichard et al., 2012, 2013) rather suggest that ring stacking in vivo is based on parallel interactions between the SAS-6 coiled-coil stalks and vertical interactions of SAS-6 associated components at the periphery of centriolar cartwheels.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent EM studies.

claim: A release of the closed Y215 SAS-6 state through either a regulatory protein or a direct phosphorylation of Y215 could provide a mechanism to trigger SAS-6 assembly locally.
source: We speculate that a release of this closed SAS-6 state through either a regulatory protein or a direct phosphorylation of Y215 could provide a simple mechanism to trigger SAS-6 assembly locally by increasing the concentration of assembly efficient SAS-6.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the structural observations of the Y215 closed state.

claim: If the Y215 regulatory mechanism is used in vivo, it would probably be confined to the Trypanosomatids.
source: Should this mechanism indeed be used in vivo (which is currently unknown), it would probably be confined to the Trypanosomatids as other SAS-6 homologues appear not to have tyrosine/aromatic residues in the position equivalent to Y215 that could play an equivalent role.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The evolutionary conservation of the hydrophobic pocket involved in dimerization together with PK9119's relatively broad activity could suggest that PK9119 targets this pocket.
source: The evolutionary conservation of the hydrophobic pocket involved in dimerization together with PK9119's relatively broad activity in inhibiting both L. major and (to a lesser extent) D. rerio SAS-6 could suggest that PK9119 targets this pocket.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on conservation analysis and inhibition data.

claim: NMR binding studies are most consistent with PK9119 binding adjacent to the head-to-head dimerization interface and thereby altering its structure subtly.
source: However, our NMR binding studies are most consistent with PK9119 binding adjacent to the head-to-head dimerization interface and thereby altering its structure subtly (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by NMR chemical shift perturbation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HADDOCK modeling suggests that 98% of docked PK9119 structures occupied a single cluster in which PK9119 was bound to helix α1, facing away from the hydrophobic pocket.
source: Confirming this notion, when we modeled the SAS-6–PK9119 complex with the HADDOCK software package (available at http://haddock.science.uu.nl/services/HADDOCK/haddock.php) (de Vries et al., 2010; Wassenaar et al., 2012), using high ambiguity restraints derived from the observed chemical shift perturbations in HSQC spectra (6 restraints >0.2 ppm), we found that of the 200 docked structures 98% occupied a single cluster in which PK9119 was bound to helix α1, but not on the side lining the hydrophobic pocket, but on its opposite side, facing away from this pocket (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling using HADDOCK.

claim: An elucidation of a high-resolution structure of PK9119 bound to its target would be important to understand how exactly PK9119 functions in inhibiting L. major SAS-6.
source: Clearly, an elucidation of a high-resolution structure of PK9119 bound to its target would be important to understand how exactly PK9119 functions in inhibiting L. major SAS-6.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: The binding affinity of PK9119 is currently low (in the mM range).
source: The binding affinity of our compound is currently low (in the mM range) and it does not show strong species specificity.
evidence: This is supported by NMR titration data.

claim: PK9119 does not show strong species specificity.
source: The binding affinity of our compound is currently low (in the mM range) and it does not show strong species specificity.
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS data showing inhibition of both L. major and zebrafish SAS-6.

claim: It will be essential to systematically explore chemical modifications of PK9119's central indole scaffold to improve binding affinity and species specificity.
source: To establish whether PK9119 has any potential to be improved in these critical aspects, it will be essential to systematically explore chemical modifications of its central indole scaffold.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: The demonstration that SAS-6 can be inhibited in vitro is a first step towards developing SAS-6 inhibitors that could be used in vivo.
source: Regardless of these limitations, our demonstration that SAS-6 can be inhibited in vitro is a first, small step towards the goal of developing SAS-6 inhibitors that also could be used in vivo, for example as a cell-biological tool.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the findings for future research.
